summary: Defines the SIP Join header, which logically joins an existing SIP dialog with a new one. It enables features such as barge-in, message screening and call center monitoring.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3911 adds a Join header to SIP so that a new caller can be put into a call that is already going on. The caller sends an invitation that names the existing conversation, and the user agent that receives it looks up that conversation, checks that the caller is allowed in, and either mixes the audio itself or moves everyone to a conference server. No central controller is needed, although one can still be used.

questions: what is the sip join header
how does sip barge in work
what does 481 mean for a join request
subtitle: A SIP header that lets a new caller join an ongoing call without a central controller.

tldr.problem: Putting a third person into a call that is already running normally needs third-party call control, which means a central point in the path that both parties talk to. That central point may not be wanted, and it does not exist in a peer-to-peer setup.
tldr.mechanism: The Join header is added to an INVITE request. It carries the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag of the dialog the sender wants to join, and the user agent that receives it looks up that dialog, checks that the sender is allowed to join, and either mixes the new participant in locally or moves the conversation to a conference server.
tldr.outcome: The header is registered for use with INVITE, and a join option tag lets a sender ask for an explicit failure if the receiver does not support it. Because a party is always aware of a join request and can decline it, the memo argues the primitive is not a wiretap in the sense of RFC 2804, though it does change the security balance of SIP and requires authentication and authorization of the joiner.

facts.label: Option tag
facts.value: join, for the Require and Supported headers

today: RFC 3911 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It registers the Join SIP header and the join option tag for the Require and Supported headers, and it was produced in the IETF SIP working group.

sections.title: What the Join Header Does
sections.content:
This document describes a SIP extension header field, as part of the SIP multiparty applications architecture framework. The Join header is used to logically join an existing SIP dialog with a new SIP dialog, which is especially useful in peer-to-peer call control environments.

One use of the Join header is to insert a new participant into a multimedia conversation, which may be a two-party call or a SIP conference. That functionality is already available using third-party call control, but that model requires a central point of control which may not be desirable in many environments, so a method of performing the same call control primitives in a distributed, peer-to-peer fashion is very desirable.

An explicit Join header is needed in some cases instead of addressing an INVITE to a conference URI. A conference may not yet exist, and the new invitation may be trying to join an ordinary two-party call. The party joining may not know whether the dialog it wants to join is part of a conference, and it may not know the conference URI.

The header enables services such as barge-in, real-time message screening and call centre monitoring in a distributed peer-to-peer way, and the list is not exhaustive.

The memo's example: the Boss has an established two-party conversation with the Customer, and using some out-of-band mechanism such as voice, gestures or email asks an Assistant to join the conversation. The Assistant sends an INVITE with a Join header to the Boss, carrying the dialog information for the established dialog, which it obtained from some other mechanism such as a web page, an instant message or the SIP session dialog package.

The operation effectively creates a new conference, and the Boss needs to cause a new conference to start, and consequently to create or obtain a new conference URI. In the example the Boss mixes all media locally, so it needs to generate a new conference URI and return it as the Contact of the Join INVITE, with the isfocus contact header field parameter, and re-INVITE or UPDATE the Customer with the conference URI as the new Contact.
sections.plainLanguage: The header names a call that is already in progress and asks to be put into it. The party that receives the request works out which conversation is meant, checks that the requester is allowed in, and then either mixes the audio itself or moves the call to a conference server.

sections.title: The WireTap Question
sections.content:
This primitive can be used to create services that are used for monitoring purposes, but those services do not meet the definition of a wiretap in RFC 2804. The memo quotes the definition: wiretapping is what occurs when information passed across the Internet from one party to one or more other parties is delivered to a third party, first without the sending party knowing about the third party, second without any of the recipient parties knowing about the delivery to the third party, third when the normal expectation of the sender is that the transmitted information will only be seen by the recipient parties or parties obliged to keep the information in confidence, and fourth when the third party acts deliberately to target the transmission of the first party, either because he is of interest, or because the second party's reception is of interest.

Specifically, item 2 does not apply to this extension, because one party is always aware of a Join request and can even decline such requests. In addition, in many applications of this primitive some or all of the other items may not apply. In many call centres that handle financial transactions, for instance, all conversations are recorded with the full knowledge and expectation of all parties involved.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo addresses the obvious question: is this a way of listening in on calls? It says no, because a party in the call always knows a join request has been made and can refuse it, and because in many uses of the header everyone knows the call is recorded.

sections.title: Receiving a Join Header
sections.content:
The Join header contains the information used to match an existing SIP dialog, which is the call-id, the to-tag and the from-tag. On receiving an INVITE with a Join header, the user agent server attempts to match this information with a confirmed or early dialog. The to-tag and from-tag parameters are matched as if they were tags in an incoming request, so the to-tag is compared to the local tag and the from-tag to the remote tag.

Several cases have to be rejected or handled in a fixed way. If more than one Join header is present in an INVITE, or a Join header is present in a request other than INVITE, the user agent server must reject the request with a 400 Bad Request response. The Join header has specific call control semantics, so if it and another header with contradictory semantics are present, for example a Replaces header, the request must be rejected with a 400 Bad Request response. If the Join header matches more than one dialog, the user agent must act as if no match is found.

If no match is found but the Request-URI of the INVITE corresponds to a conference URI, the user agent server must ignore the Join header and carry on processing the INVITE as if it did not exist, which lets a user agent that receives an INVITE with Join redirect the request straight to a conference URI. Otherwise, if no match is found, the user agent server rejects the INVITE with a 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist response, and the same goes if the Join header matches a dialog that was not created with an INVITE. If it matches a dialog that has already terminated, the user agent should decline the request with a 603 Declined response.

If the Join header matches an active dialog, and unlike the Replaces header the Join header has no limitation on its use with early dialogs, the user agent must verify that the initiator of the new INVITE is authorized to join the matched dialog. If the initiator has authenticated successfully as equivalent to the user being joined, the join is authorized: for example if the user being joined and the initiator of the joining dialog share the same credentials for Digest authentication, or if they sign the join request with S/MIME using the same private key and present the same certificate as in the original dialog.

Alternatively, the Referred-By mechanism gives the user agent a way to verify that a join request was sent on behalf of the other participant in the matched dialog, for instance triggered by a REFER request. If the join request contains a Referred-By header corresponding to the user being joined, the user agent should treat the join as authorized by the joined party. The Referred-By header must reference a corresponding, valid Referred-By Authenticated Identity Body. The user agent may apply other local policy to the remainder of the request, so it may apply different policy to the joined dialog than was applied to the target dialog.

The user agent may also maintain a list of authorized entities allowed to join any dialog with certain characteristics, for instance all the dialogs in the call centre context of the user agent, and it may use other authorization mechanisms defined for the purpose in standards track extensions, such as a mechanism for transitively asserting authorization of a join.

If authorization succeeds, the user agent attempts to accept the new INVITE and assign whatever mixing or conferencing resources are needed. If it cannot accept the new INVITE, for example because it cannot establish the required quality of service or keying, or because it has incompatible media, it must return an appropriate error response and must leave the matched dialog unchanged.

A user agent that accepts a Join header needs to set up dialogs or conferences so that the requesting user agent client is logically added to the conversation space associated with the matched dialog, and any dialogs already logically associated with the matched dialog in the same conversation space are included as well. If the user agent server has enough resources to handle the request locally, it should accept the request and perform the appropriate media mixing or combining, and it may instead rearrange the appropriate dialogs as described below, based on local policy.

If it does not have enough local resources, or does not wish to use them, but knows of other resources that could satisfy the request, such as a centralized conference server, the user agent should create a conference using that resource, redirect the requestor to it, and ask the other participants in the same conversation space to use it as well. Any appropriate mechanism may be used to move the participants, such as a 3xx response, third-party call control re-invitations, REFER requests, or re-invitations to a multicast group, but only mechanisms that are expected to be acceptable to the other participants should be used. A user agent should not try to move participants to a multicast group unless it can reasonably expect all of them to support multicast. If the user agent server is incapable of satisfying the Join request at all, it must return a 488 Not Acceptable Here response.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver looks for a call matching the identifiers in the header, and has a fixed answer for each outcome: a malformed request gets 400, no matching call gets 481, a call that has already ended gets 603, and a call it cannot join gets 488. Before allowing the join, it must check that the requester is entitled to join, either because they proved they are the same user or because the other party referred them.

sections.title: Sending a Join Header and Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
A user agent that wishes to add a new dialog of its own to a single existing early or confirmed dialog, and any associated dialogs or conferences, may send the target user agent an INVITE request containing a Join header. The user agent client places the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag information for the target dialog in a single Join header and sends the new INVITE to the target.

If the user agent receives a 300-class response and acts on it by sending an INVITE to a Contact in the response, that redirected INVITE must contain the same Join header as the original request. The memo notes that this is unusual, but it allows INVITE requests with a Join header to be redirected before reaching the target user agent server.

The memo is explicit about a limitation: the Join mechanism provides no way to match multiple dialogs, no way to match an entire call, an entire transaction, or to follow a chain of proxy forking logic.

Proxy servers need no new behaviour for this extension. They simply pass the Join header transparently, as the SIP specification describes. The memo does note that a proxy, especially one forking on application layer logic such as caller screening or time-of-day routing, may forward an INVITE containing a Join header to a completely orthogonal set of Contacts from the original request it was meant to replace, in which case the request with the Join header will fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender puts the identifiers of the call it wants to join into the invitation. If the invitation is redirected on the way, the header has to be copied into the new invitation. Proxies just pass the header along, though a proxy that forks the request can send it somewhere the join will not work.

sections.title: The Syntax of the Header
sections.content:
The Join header field indicates that a new dialog, created by the INVITE in which the header is contained, should be joined with the dialog identified by the header field, and any associated dialogs or conferences. It is a request header only, and is defined only for INVITE requests. It may be encrypted as part of end-to-end encryption, and only a single Join header field value may be present in a SIP request.

The syntax uses the augmented Backus-Naur Form of RFC 2234. A Join header is the word Join, a colon, a callid, and any number of semicolon-separated join parameters, which are a to-tag, a from-tag, or a generic parameter. A to-tag is the literal to-tag, an equals sign and a token, and a from-tag is the literal from-tag, an equals sign and a token.

A Join header must contain exactly one to-tag and exactly one from-tag, because they are required for unique dialog matching. For compatibility with dialogs initiated by user agents compliant with RFC 2543, a to-tag of zero matches both a to-tag value of zero and a null to-tag, and likewise a from-tag of zero matches both a from-tag value of zero and a null from-tag.

The memo gives three examples: a Join header with the call identifier as a SIP URI and the two tags on continuation lines, a Join header with a bare call identifier and both tags in parameters, and a Join header with an IP address, a to-tag and a from-tag of zero.

The specification also defines a new option tag, join, for the Require and Supported headers. User agents that support the Join header must include the join option tag in a Supported header field, and user agents that want explicit failure notification if Join is not supported may include the join option in a Require header field, as in Require: join, 100rel.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries the identifier of the call and the two tags that make it unique. It may only appear once, and only in an invitation. A separate option tag, join, lets a sender say in advance that it wants to be told if the receiver cannot do joins.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension specified in the memo significantly changes the relative security of SIP devices. Currently in SIP, even if an eavesdropper learns the Call-ID, To and From headers of a dialog, they cannot easily modify or destroy that dialog if Digest authentication or end-to-end message integrity are used.

The extension can be used to insert or monitor potentially sensitive content in a multimedia conversation. Invitations with the Join header must therefore only be accepted if the peer requesting the join has been properly authenticated using a standard SIP mechanism, Digest or S/MIME, and authorized to be joined with the target dialog. All SIP implementations are already required to support Digest authentication. Generally, authorization for joins is configured as a matter of local policy as long-duration persistent relationships.

The memo's examples of such policy: the user agents used by call centre agents might be configured with a list of identities that could join their calls, such as supervisors and any call centre monitoring user agents, and the agents might instead rely on transitive authorization assertions from a shorter list of authorized hosts such as a certificate authority. For answering-machine-style message screening it is even easier, because the user screening their messages presumably already has some credentials with the messaging server.

Some mechanisms for obtaining the dialog information the header needs, the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag, include URIs on a web page, subscriptions to an appropriate event package, and notifications after a REFER request. The use of end-to-end security mechanisms to integrity protect and encrypt this information is also recommended.

The extension was designed to take advantage of future signature or authorization schemes defined by standards track extensions, and in general call control features would benefit considerably from such work. Section 4 of the memo describes the specific mechanisms for authorization using Digest authentication, S/MIME and Referred-By, which are the capabilities currently available in SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the header lets a stranger into a call, the receiver must check who is asking, both that they proved who they are and that they are allowed in. The memo says the usual rules of SIP can do this, and that a site should decide in advance which identities may join which calls.

viz.caption: Illustrative, not from the RFC: the assistant joining the boss's call

messages.label: INVITE with Join
messages.note: The assistant sends a new invitation carrying the identifiers of the call already in progress.

messages.label: re-INVITE
messages.note: The boss re-invites the customer so that the customer learns the new conference URI.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: The boss accepts the join and returns the conference URI as the contact.

messages.label: ACK
messages.note: The assistant acknowledges, and the media of the three participants begins to mix.

viz.caption: THE RESPONSES A JOIN CAN PRODUCE

items.label: Bad Request
items.desc: More than one Join header, a Join header in a request other than INVITE, or a header with contradictory semantics such as Replaces.

items.label: Call/Transaction Does Not Exist
items.desc: No dialog matched the header, or the matched dialog was not created with an INVITE.

items.label: Declined
items.desc: The matched dialog has already terminated.

items.label: Not Acceptable Here
items.desc: The user agent cannot satisfy the join request at all.

items.label: Busy
items.desc: Used in the rejected example, where the party does not want to be disturbed.

items.label: Moved Temporarily
items.desc: Used when the request is redirected to a conference created for the join.

data.title: Join header syntax and examples
data.code:
Join            = "Join" HCOLON callid *(SEMI join-param)
join-param      = to-tag / from-tag / generic-param
to-tag          = "to-tag" EQUAL token
from-tag        = "from-tag" EQUAL token

Join: 98732@sip.example.com
       ;from-tag=r33th4x0r
       ;to-tag=ff87ff

Join: 12adf2f34456gs5;to-tag=12345;from-tag=54321

Join: 87134@192.0.2.23;to-tag=24796;from-tag=0

items.title: Digest
items.text: The joining party authenticates with the same credentials as the user being joined.

items.title: S/MIME
items.text: The join request is signed with the same private key and the same certificate used in the original dialog.

items.title: Referred-By
items.text: A Referred-By header matching the user being joined counts as authorization, as after a REFER.

items.title: Local policy
items.text: The user agent may keep a list of identities allowed to join, such as supervisors in a call centre.
